overview: Imagine walking toward Mathura beside the Yamuna around 450 BCE. Dust lifts from the road, potters turn red and gray clay into bowls, and small houses cluster on floors packed with mud. This is Surasena, one of northern India's territorial states, sitting where routes linked the Ganga plain, Rajasthan and central India. Buddhist tradition remembers a king of Madhura debating whether birth made one group better than another. Archaeology offers firmer but quieter clues: postholes, painted gray bowls, black polished sherds, a bone arrowhead, terracotta discs, an amulet and broken objects catalogued as styli. They reveal work, meals, belief and danger, but do not name a dynasty. Later poems made Mathura inseparable from Krishna, while a damaged inscription centuries afterward honored five Vrishni heroes. Those sources matter only when kept in their own dates. The atlas draws Surasena from 500 to 400 BCE, yet its polygon misses nearby Sonkh and Govardhan and stretches far east. At 400 it replaces Surasena with a generic layer, so no exact final conqueror can be read from that seam. Mathura and its memories continued long after the name Surasena vanished from this map.

periods.title: The atlas opens on Surasena
periods.summary: The exact record begins at 500 BCE around Mathura. Excavated Mathura levels dated broadly from the sixth to late fourth century BCE contain simple floors, postholes and several pottery traditions, but no foundation tablet announcing a Surasena state.

periods.title: Routes and landscapes shape the polity
periods.summary: Mathura stood where northern and southern routes met, between settled farming and pasture toward Malwa. University synthesis connects that varied landscape with multiple clans and chiefs rather than one securely reconstructed centralized ministry.

periods.title: A king survives in remembered debate
periods.summary: The Madhura Sutta remembers King Avantiputta visiting Mahakaccana to ask about inherited status. The tradition is valuable for political and social memory, but it does not securely date his reign within the atlas century.

periods.title: Madhura gets an ancient bad review
periods.summary: A compact Buddhist passage complains of uneven ground, dust, fierce dogs, troublesome spirits and hard-to-find alms at Madhura. It is vivid place-memory, not a measured city survey or proof that every street shared those conditions.

periods.title: Craft and exchange leave durable traces
periods.summary: Pottery, terracotta, shell, bone and possible writing implements show a connected settlement economy. These objects reveal skilled work and exchange more safely than they reveal the names, offices or ethnic identities of their makers.

periods.title: Later sacred memory must stay later
periods.summary: Later literature strongly identifies Mathura with Krishna, while archaeological evidence for a Krishna-centered cult becomes clear much later. The card preserves both traditions without turning later devotion into an eyewitness report from 450 BCE.

periods.title: Urban works grow beyond the snapshot
periods.summary: Reassessment places Mathura mud defenses and major water and drainage works mainly around the late fourth and third centuries BCE. They show the city's continued growth, but most should not be backdated into Surasena's exact atlas interval.

periods.title: A generic layer replaces the name
periods.summary: At 400 BCE the atlas removes Surasena and assigns Mathura and every tested nearby point to a broad Hindu Kingdoms layer. That is a display seam, not evidence for a conquest by a polity of that generic name.

sections.title: First audit the exact atlas record

items.text: The exact indexed identity is id “surasena,” label “Surasena,” circa 500 to 400 BCE, generated from historical basemaps. It had one observed border interval and no existing card or override when audited. Vedic Indo-Aryans, Kuru, Pancala, Vatsa, Avanti, Magadha and Maurya remain distinct records.

At 500 BCE the target is one Polygon with one ring and 15 positions. Its bounds are 77.557° to 80.646° east and 24.749° to 28.532° north. The exact coordinate SHA-256 is 2b048cb2b5325e58621b0cf937ae88cad7094aaed236097da12288707e1e92c2. This identifies imported geometry, not an ancient survey.

Point tests place Mathura, Vrindavan, Bateshwar and Agra inside. Sonkh, Govardhan, Bharatpur, Bayana, Delhi, Hastinapura, Ahichchhatra, Kampilya, Kaushambi, Ayodhya, Varanasi, Rajgir, Ujjain and Vidisha fall outside. A digital point test does not prove every village's allegiance or ancient boundary marker.

The imported shape has a material mismatch: it excludes Sonkh and Govardhan, sites central to Mathura-region archaeology and later sacred geography, yet stretches southeast toward Bateshwar and Agra and east to longitude 80.646°. The card preserves the exact polygon while warning against treating it as a recovered frontier.

The exact id is absent at 700, 400, 323 and 300 BCE. A broad Vedic layer precedes it; a generic Hindu Kingdoms layer follows at 400; Magadha covers the audited region at 323; Maurya covers it at 300. These snapshots cannot name a direct conqueror.

Surasena appears among the northern mahajanapadas, with Mathura or Madhura as its capital on the Yamuna. The atlas opens midway through a longer regional history. Its 500 BCE boundary is map coverage, not the birth date of Mathura, its population or a dynasty.

Excavated Mathura contains occupation before, during and long after the atlas century. An object “from Mathura” is not automatically Surasena-period. Stratigraphic level, pottery association and scientific or comparative dating matter more than the modern label attached to the excavation box.

Sonkh lies roughly thirty kilometers southwest of Mathura and preserves a deep multi-period mound. It belongs to the regional archaeological story but falls outside the exact atlas polygon. Its evidence can illuminate neighboring life only when its location and dating limits are stated.

Buddhist texts, epic and Puranic traditions, archaeology and later inscriptions answer different questions. A remembered debate may preserve social ideas; a potsherd proves material activity; an inscription can name a donor centuries later. None should silently substitute for another kind of evidence.

Later authors made Mathura a central landscape of Krishna's childhood and the Vrishnis. That memory is historically important, but clear inscriptions and cult images are later than 500 to 400 BCE. The card never treats a later sacred biography as a dated Surasena court chronicle.

sections.title: Politics, diplomacy and war remain unevenly known

items.text: University synthesis describes Andhakas, Vrishnis and other groups in the Mathura region and proposes a samgha-like organization with several chiefs. Buddhist tradition also remembers a king, Avantiputta. Together they suggest changing or mixed political forms, not a tidy constitution recoverable article by article.

Avantiputta arrives to meet Mahakaccana in royal vehicles and asks about Brahmin claims to superiority. The teacher answers that wealth, service, punishment and moral conduct cross inherited categories. The scene reveals remembered kingship and argument, but Avantiputta lacks a securely dated independent royal inscription.

Territorial states raised revenue from farming, craft and exchange and maintained officials and armed forces. Applying this broad pattern to Surasena is reasonable; inventing named departments, tax rates or a permanent troop count is not. No contemporary Surasena administrative archive survives.

A bone arrowhead from Mathura's early levels provides direct evidence for projectile technology, hunting or conflict, though its exact use is unknown. Later defenses show organized power around the city, but they are mainly later than the atlas interval and cannot prove a particular Surasena war.

No consulted source provides a secure last Surasena ruler, surrender treaty or battle in 400 BCE. Magadha's later regional coverage and Mauryan rule show a larger political transformation, but the exact route from Surasena to those states remains uncertain. The ending therefore carries no automatic successor link.

Mathura's period dated roughly from the sixth century to the late fourth BCE has at least two structural subperiods. Excavators found packed floors, postholes and part of a mud platform. These modest remains show repeated building and repair, an achievement easily missed beside later stone monuments.

Painted Gray Ware bowls and dishes carried simple geometric designs. Red ware, black-and-red ware, plain gray ware and a small amount of Northern Black Polished Ware appeared too. Potters controlled clay, firing and surface treatment, but vessel style alone cannot identify a person's language or clan.

Terracotta discs, a terracotta amulet, a conch fragment, the bone arrowhead and two broken objects catalogued as styli came from early Mathura levels. Their variety points to craft, adornment, belief and tools. A catalogue label is not proof that the “styli” wrote school lessons.

At Sonkh, the earliest sequence included Painted Gray Ware and later settlement rebuilding. A hearth beside a red-ware pot offers a close material glimpse of cooking, while changing house traces warn that light structures may disappear. Sonkh is comparative regional evidence, not geometry magically moved inside Surasena.

Archaeology's achievement is chronological: floors, pits, pottery and later walls are separated into layers instead of blended into one “ancient Mathura.” That method shows why the city's famous stone sculpture, wells, fortification and Krishna-related monuments belong mostly to later phases rather than this card's century.

sections.title: Farms, herds, workshops and routes support Mathura

items.text: Mathura stood at a junction between the northern Uttarapatha corridor and routes toward central and western India. The Yamuna linked it to the Ganga plain. Travelers, carts, pack animals and river movement carried goods and news, though surviving evidence cannot calculate annual Surasena trade volume.

Farming and herding supported territorial states. Broader northern evidence includes rice, barley, wheat, pulses, sesame, cattle and other animals. This gives a responsible regional range, not a preserved Mathura shopping list. Pasture toward Malwa likely mattered alongside settled fields nearer the Yamuna.

Iron axes, hoes, sickles, knives, nails, weapons and craft tools expanded what farmers, builders and smiths could do. Surasena did not invent iron, and access varied. Skilled production, repair and repeated use mattered more than a single dramatic “iron revolution.”

Fine and coarse pottery served different tasks: displaying or serving food, cooking, hauling and storing. Clay vessels also moved between workshops and markets. Their distribution reveals exchange, but one glossy sherd cannot prove long-distance travel or identify whether its owner was a farmer, merchant or chief.

Conch, bone, terracotta and carefully finished pottery imply supply chains and specialized skill. A shell fragment may have traveled far from the sea before reaching Mathura. The object proves movement of material more securely than it proves the route, price or identity of the trader who carried it.

sections.title: Belief and learning travel by voice

items.text: Vedic rites, household practices, renunciant debates and emerging Buddhist and Jain communities belonged to the wider age. Mathura later became a major center for several traditions. Religious plurality does not mean each tradition had the same strength in 450 BCE or that every household believed alike.

The Pali opening “Evaṃ me sutaṃ ... āyasmā Mahākaccāno Madhurāyaṃ viharati Gundāvane” means, “Thus have I heard ... Venerable Mahakaccana was staying near Madhura in Gundavana.” It is a carefully transmitted oral-text setting, not writing excavated from a Surasena palace at all.

The Madhura discussion challenges claims that birth alone makes Brahmins superior. Its examples ask who can hire servants, receive punishment or live morally. It is valuable evidence for remembered social argument, while its transmission history prevents us from assigning every sentence to one securely dated public meeting.

Vedic learning required exact sound, accent and ordered recitation. Some pupils began young and practiced intensively with teachers. That was demanding specialist education, not universal schooling. Most children learned household work, language, customs and crafts through close observation and participation.

Ancient education ideals emphasize memorization, discussion, discipline and close teacher-pupil relationships. No consulted source identifies a public Mathura school, literacy percentage, girls' syllabus or daily class timetable for 500 to 400 BCE. The two possible styli are intriguing, not a school register.

sections.title: Families, women and children lived within rank

items.text: Households joined care, production and ritual, often under patrilineal ideals and male authority. Several generations might cooperate, but postholes cannot reveal a family tree. Direct Surasena marriage contracts, birth lists, inheritance files and household censuses do not survive, so family size and residence patterns remain uncertain.

Varna ideals ranked Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, while an actual town also needed farmers, herders, traders, potters, smiths, laborers, servants and religious specialists. Wealth, occupation, age, gender and local ties shaped status; a four-part ideal was not a perfect street census.

Women processed food, carried water, managed textiles, cared for children and animals, exchanged goods and joined household ritual. Elite texts often centered men, leaving ordinary women's decisions faint. Surasena-specific evidence for property, inheritance, childbirth care and girls' education is too sparse for universal rules.

The later Mora inscription was commissioned by a person named Tosa or Tosha, often interpreted as a woman, for a Vrishni shrine. It shows later female patronage near Mathura, centuries after this card's interval. It cannot prove that every Surasena woman had comparable wealth or religious freedom.

Children probably fetched water or fuel, watched animals, processed grain, minded younger siblings and learned crafts in stages; a minority entered intensive recitation training. This is an inference from household economies and oral education. Archaeology has not recovered a Surasena chore chart, report card or fixed working age.

sections.title: Homes, meals, clothing, work and play leave scraps

items.text: Packed mud floors, postholes and a partial platform imply light buildings repeatedly repaired. Walls and roofs may have used mud, timber, reeds or thatch, materials that decay unevenly. Later brick buildings cannot simply be copied backward. Rural shelters probably survive even less clearly than town structures.

Grain, pulses, milk products, oils, fruits and vegetables supplied possible meals across northern India, while meat and fish varied by group and circumstance. Grinding, pounding, cooking and cleaning took time. Pots survive more easily than recipes, so there is no exact “Surasena lunchbox.”

Cloth rarely survives, but broader evidence supports wrapped garments, shawls, belts and ornaments of shell, terracotta, bead, metal or stone. Exact colors, cuts and children's sizes at Surasena are unknown. A conch fragment can outlive the string, wearer and fashion advice that once gave it meaning.

Farmers, herders, potters, smiths, builders, traders, carters and household workers kept the settlement running. Tasks overlapped: a farmer could mend tools, a household could spin thread, and traders could travel seasonally. The sources do not preserve wages, working hours or a complete Mathura job list.

Children and adults could sing, tell stories, race, wrestle or use simple counters and toys, but specific Mathura rules rarely survive. A small clay disc might be a counter, spindle whorl, lid, ritual piece or toy. Ancient people also misplaced things whose instruction manuals vanished.

sections.title: Healing, water and toilets require candor

items.text: Early healing combined plant substances, foods, water, ointments, fumigation, practical observation and ritual speech. Buddhist literature later remembers recognizable physicians and nursing. The famous systematic medical compendia were compiled over time, so their finished recipes should not be dropped whole into a Mathura home of 450 BCE.

No consulted excavation identifies a Surasena-period clinic, surgeon's room, midwife's kit or pharmacy inventory. Illness, injury, childbirth and caregiving certainly existed, probably handled first in households and sometimes by specialists. Evidence cannot provide local survival rates or turn every pointed bone object into medical equipment.

The Yamuna was central to Mathura's location, but river access did not guarantee clean water. People likely used carried water, local wells or storage vessels according to place and means. Securely dated target-period water installations are sparse, so universal taps, protected wells or treatment systems cannot be claimed.

Later Mathura phases used ring wells, drains and other water or waste devices, while broader early Indian archaeology records soakage arrangements. Most substantial Mathura examples belong after the atlas century. They demonstrate continued urban planning, not a citywide Surasena sewer installed before 400 BCE.

No ordinary household toilet, latrine seat or sewer is securely identified for Surasena's exact interval in the consulted reports. Waste may have gone to pits, open ground or removed containers, but direct proof is thin. Dusty streets in a Buddhist complaint are vivid evidence, not a sanitation inspection score.

sections.title: Read later writing and follow continuity carefully

items.text: Authentic later Mathura-area sample, about the early first century CE, displayed as readable normalized Brahmi Unicode: “𑀪𑀕𑀯𑀢𑀸𑀁 𑀯𑀾𑀱𑁆𑀡𑀺𑀦𑀸𑀁 𑀧𑀁𑀘𑀯𑀺𑀭𑀸𑀡𑀁 𑀧𑁆𑀭𑀢𑀺𑀫𑀸𑀂”. Modern Unicode regularizes damaged and variable letterforms; it is not a photograph or facsimile.

Epigraphic transliteration: “bhagavatāṃ Vṛṣṇinā(m) paṃcavirāṇaṃ pratimā[h].” A readable normalized Sanskrit form is “bhagavatāṃ vṛṣṇīnāṃ pañcavīrāṇāṃ pratimāḥ.” Compact translation: “images of the blessed five heroes of the Vrishnis.” Parentheses and brackets mark uncertain or restored letters in the damaged stone.

The Mora well inscription came from a village west of Mathura and refers to images in a stone shrine. It belongs roughly five centuries after the Surasena atlas snapshot. Its language and script document later Vrishni worship near Mathura, not the spoken language, writing habits or Krishna biography of 450 BCE.

The inscription is damaged, its five heroes have been interpreted in different ways, and the visible text has deteriorated since early recording. Showing a short phrase with editorial marks is more honest than pretending the whole monument is perfectly readable. The original script also differs from modern printed Brahmi glyphs.

At 400 BCE the atlas substitutes a generic layer; at 323 it maps Magadha; at 300 it maps Maurya. Mathura continued as a city, route center and many-tradition sacred landscape. Surasena ends here as an uncertain named polity, while its place, people and later Vrishni memory continue without a falsely exact conquest story.

ending.text: The atlas stops drawing Surasena at about 400 BCE and replaces it around Mathura with a generic Hindu Kingdoms layer. By 323 BCE the audited region is mapped as Magadha and by 300 as Maurya, but those later snapshots do not identify one conqueror or prove a transfer in exactly 400 BCE. No consulted source supplies a secure last Surasena ruler, surrender treaty or final battle. Mathura itself continued to grow as a route center and a place of Buddhist, Jain, Brahmanical and later Krishna-related traditions. The structured ending is therefore uncertain at the atlas seam, with no direct successor link. That preserves the distinction between disappearance of a map label, loss or transformation of a polity, and the much longer life of the city and its people.
